pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. et al. 
Docket Nos. EL25-49-000 
Large Load Co-Located at Generating 
Facilities 
AD24-11-111 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC  
v.  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
EL25-20-000  
(Consolidated) 
 
ANSWER OF PPL ELECTRIC UTILTIIES CORPORATION 
 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules and Regulations of the Federal Energy Regu-
latory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”),1 and pursuant to the instructions in the Order to 
Show Cause,2 PPL Electric Utilities Corporation (“PPL Electric”) hereby submits this Answer to 
the PJM Answer3 as well as other answers submitted in this docket.4 
 
1 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 213 (2025).  
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115, ¶ 87 (Feb. 20, 2025) (“Order to Show Cause”) (in-
structing “interested entities” to respond within 30 days of PJM and the transmission owners’ filings “ad-
dressing either or both of: (1) whether the existing Tariff remains just and reasonable and not unduly dis-
criminatory or preferential; and (2) if not, what changes to the Tariff should be implemented as replace-
ment rates.”).  
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket Nos. EL25-49-000 et al. 
(Mar. 24, 2025) (“PJM Answer”).  
4 PPL Electric also responds to Answers submitted by PSE&G, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., Re-
sponse of Public Service Electric and Gas Company to the Order to Show Cause, Docket Nos. EL25-49 et

1 
 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The electric industry is now well into its second year of intense focus on large loads co-
locating with wholesale generators. The Commission has numerous dockets, open and closed, on 
the subject and has held an all-day technical conference where it heard detailed testimony from 
industry experts on all sides of the question. Although the technical, jurisdictional, and economic 
issues are complex, the Commission can best proceed if it follows two hopefully non-controver-
sial “North Star” principles:  
(1) 
Protect the safety and reliability of the bulk electric system; and  
(2) 
Prevent subsidization of new loads by network customers.   
Guided by these principles, and utilizing the extensive records before it, the Commission can 
take action to clarify its rules around behind-the-meter loads at regulated wholesale generators.  
 
In its Answer, PJM brings its experience—developed over several years of grappling 
with these issues—to the myriad questions presented by co-location. PJM recognizes that there 
are limits to its ability to stop behind-the-meter load from interconnecting to the wholesale gen-
erators interconnected with the grid. As a federally regulated public utility, PJM has no jurisdic-
tion over these retail questions. In several PJM states, state law allows such behind-the-meter re-
tail load. Instead, PJM focuses on what it can control: its own Tariff. Specifically, PJM defends 
the justness and reasonableness of the Tariff, but it recognizes that the rules of the road can be 
unclear in certain cases. It outlines eight potential Options for large loads co-located with whole-
sale generators. Four of these are already permitted by the Tariff (but may still benefit from 
 
al. (Mar. 24, 2025) (“PSE&G Answer”) and AES Ohio, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., Answer of 
the Dayton Power and Light Company d/b/a AES Ohio to Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 
206 of the Federal Power Act and Consolidating with Other Proceedings, Docket Nos. EL25-49, et al. 
(Mar. 24, 2025) (“AES Ohio Answer”).

2 
 
clarification when applied to behind-the-meter load) and four would require some degree of 
amendment to the Tariff. Not all are equally desirable. In fact, PJM explicitly says that it does 
not prefer the options that relieve behind-the-meter load of its network obligations. It also ex-
plains why: this load cannot be fully isolated and inevitably brings operational risk to the system. 
Nevertheless, such accommodation may be required by state law. PJM is obligated to do so in a 
way that minimizes these risks.  
 
PPL Electric agrees with PJM. The PJM Tariff is already just and reasonable. But, there 
are clearly areas where the PJM Tariff (and other FERC-regulated tariffs) could benefit from in-
creased clarity and FERC guidance. Because the Commission has shown skepticism toward ad-
dressing these questions through bespoke language in non-conforming interconnection agree-
ments, it is appropriate to set these rules of the road directly in the tariffs. The Commission 
should not do so by mandating changes through this § 206 proceeding, but instead should issue 
detailed guiding principles that PJM and other tariff administrators can incorporate utilizing their 
§ 205 authority. PPL Electric believes that these rules can, and should, accommodate behind-the-
meter load where required by state law, without violating the North Star principles laid out 
above.  
II. 
BACKGROUND 
 
PPL Electric is a Pennsylvania transmission and distribution utility, and a founding mem-
ber of PJM. PPL Electric’s interest in co-located load was laid out in detail in its Post-Technical 
Conference Comments in Docket No. AD24-11, consolidated into this docket and incorporated 
by reference here.5 In addition to its general interest as a PJM transmission owner and market 
 
5 Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities, Post Technical Conference Comments of PPL Elec-
tric Utilities Corporation (“PPL Electric TC Comments”), Docket No. AD24-11-000 (Dec. 9, 2024).

3 
 
participant, PPL Electric shares an electrical interconnection with its former affiliate at the Sus-
quehanna Steam Electric Station (“Susquehanna”). For the last five years, Susquehanna has been 
working, at first alone and later with contractual partners, to develop on-site, co-located load at 
its generation facility. Importantly, the load at Susquehanna, initially a crypto-mining facility and 
more recently a large data center, was installed behind the Susquehanna meter. Rather than being 
interconnected with the local utility, PPL Electric, and purchasing from a PJM wholesale sup-
plier, as is normal for large customers in Pennsylvania, the customer instead purchases power di-
rectly from Susquehanna in a private transaction.  
 
Susquehanna and its parent company Talen Energy, as well as other generators, have 
long sought clarity from PJM related to how its Tariff would treat questions of behind-the-meter 
load. In a familiar, if unproductive, process, PJM presented questions to its stakeholders, noting 
the Tariff lacked clarity and presenting a problem statement and issue charge.6 The stakeholder 
process was unable to come to consensus on any contentious issues and largely went nowhere.7 
Instead, Susquehanna informed PJM and PPL Electric of the changes to its wholesale intercon-
nection caused by the behind-the-meter load and worked with them to accommodate those 
changes in its Interconnection Service Agreement (the “Susquehanna ISA”).  
 
After a few years, PJM unilaterally developed and posted a Guidance Document on Co-
Located Load Configurations in March 2024.8 The Guidance Document, which was clearly in-
formed by lessons learned at Susquehanna, allowed PJM to express its clear, consistent prefer-
ences regarding co-located load:  
 
6 See generally, PPL Electric TC Comments, Note 5 at 6–7.  
7 Id.  
8 Id. at 6–7.

4 
 
• 
It should be served in front of the meter.  
• 
Behind-the-meter load will not be considered network load and will not receive 
the benefits of network service. Generators installing behind-the-meter load will 
have to reduce their capacity injection rights and load must have system protec-
tions in place to protect the transmission system.  
• 
Non-network load cannot become network load without going through the various 
study processes.9  
PPL Electric shared many of the goals of the Guidance Document and supported PJM’s efforts to 
incorporate its guidance into the Susquehanna ISA. Following the November 1, 2024, denial of 
the Susquehanna ISA and the technical conference on co-located load, PJM withdrew its Guid-
ance Document pending FERC action in this matter.10   
 
The instant docket was initiated on February 20, 2025, when FERC issued the Order to 
Show Cause11 and consolidated several other dockets for further consideration. Using its § 206 
authority, the Commission found that the PJM Tariff “appears to be unjust, unreasonable, unduly 
discriminatory or preferential” and directed PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners to show 
cause why the Tariff remains just and reasonable “without provisions addressing with sufficient 
 
9 See PJM Guidance on Co-located Load Configurations (Updated Apr. 17, 2024), available at 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/pjm-guidance-on-co-located-load.ashx. 
See also, Co-Located Load Guidance, MIC Presentation (Apr. 3, 2024), available at 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/commit-tees-groups/committees/mic/2024/20240403/20240403-item-07---
co-located-load-guidance.ashx, and MRC Presentation (Apr. 25, 2024), available at 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/committees-groups/commit-tees/mrc/2024/20240425/20240425-item-09---
1-co-located-load-guidance---presentation.ashx.   
10 After several changes to the Susquehanna ISA were accepted without incident, a broader set of changes 
was protested and ultimately rejected by the Commission. See Order Rejecting Amendments to Intercon-
nection Service Agreement, 189 FERC ¶ 61,078, Docket No. ER21-2172 (Nov. 1, 2024) (“ISA Rejection 
Order”); upheld on rehearing, Order Addressing Argument on Rehearing and Granting Clarification, in 
Part, 191 FERC ¶ 61,025 (Apr. 10, 2025).  
11 Order to Show Cause, Note 2, supra.

5 
 
clarity or consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to co-location arrange-
ments.”12 Alternatively, they were to “explain what changes … would remedy the identified con-
cerns.”13  
 
PJM responded to the Order to Show Cause on March 24 with an Answer stating that the 
Tariff was just and reasonable, a detailed analysis of the policy issues related to co-located load 
(still largely reflective of the Guidance Document principles), and a presentation of potential 
paths forward. PJM stated that its approach to large loads, co-located or not, focuses on (1) re-
source adequacy, (2) reliable operations, (3) facilitating load integration, and (4) providing infor-
mation to support equitable transmission costs.14 PJM’s preference remains that all load be con-
sidered Network Load. PJM conceded that there is some uncertainty in the Tariff and there may 
be call for clarification, especially if states allow co-location of retail load behind the generation 
meters.15 The PJM Answer provides eight Options in its Answer. It recognizes that not all are 
equally desirable and some may be prohibited, at least in some states. In many cases, more than 
one option can function simultaneously. The first three and eighth options are already permitted 
by the Tariff while the other four will likely require amendments.  
 
The PJM Transmission Owners also responded to the Show Cause Order. PPL Electric 
joined nearly every other PJM Transmission Owner in a joint Answer defending the justness and 
reasonableness of the PJM Tariff and rejecting subsidization by network load. As demonstrated 
in the response being filed today by the same group of transmission owners, that is the strong, 
consistent view of the overwhelming majority of the transmission owners in PJM. Only one, 
 
12 Id. at ¶ 2.  
13 Id.  
14 PJM Answer at 3. 
15 PJM Answer at 4.

6 
 
PSE&G, disagreed with this core position, arguing instead that co-located load should receive a 
discount on transmission service because it does not burden the grid the same as normal network 
load.16  
 
PPL Electric remains in agreement with the other PJM Transmission Owners in defend-
ing the justness and reasonableness of the PJM Tariff and joins their reply being filed today. PPL 
Electric writes separately to respond more directly to PJM’s outlining of the jurisdictional and 
policy issues and the various options available. Specifically, PPL Electric’s experience at Sus-
quehanna gives it unique insight into the pitfalls of Options 4 and 5. While continuing to defend 
the justness and reasonableness of the PJM Tariff, PPL Electric agrees that FERC should provide 
additional clarity as to how federally regulated utilities should treat behind-the-meter co-located 
load where state law allows it.  
III. 
ANSWER 
A. 
Responses to PJM 
 
PPL Electric’s experience with the Susquehanna ISA and with the failure of the stake-
holder process to establish rules for behind-the-meter load brings it to the same conclusion drawn 
by PJM: “What PJM and the industry need now is Commission guidance on a path forward 
based on the record developed in this proceeding. The record will support a finding that PJM’s 
existing Tariff remains just and reasonable, although improvements and clarifications may be ap-
propriate based on Commission guidance.”17 
 
16 PSE&G Answer at 15. Other transmission owners filed shorter responses without detailed substantive 
discussion of co-located load.  
17 PJM Answer at 4.

7 
 
 
As an initial matter, the PJM Answer accurately pinpoints the potential jurisdictional 
gaps that led to the situation at Susquehanna.18 Under prevailing Pennsylvania law, a single gen-
erator providing service to a single customer is not a public utility and is not subject to the retail 
jurisdiction of the Pennsylvania Public Utilities Commission.19 As this Commission is undoubt-
edly aware, public utilities throughout the country have a long history of vigorously defending 
their state franchises to provide retail service. However, in this case, PPL Electric was not con-
sulted or given the opportunity to serve what soon became (by a large margin) the single largest 
retail customer in its service territory.20 Instead, that behind-the-meter service was simply estab-
lished by private contract. Sovereign states can allow, explicitly or implicitly, behind-the-meter 
load at generators. However, as PJM points out, the Commission retains jurisdiction over the 
transmission system and the interstate energy markets.21 While it cannot (or at least should not) 
infringe on the states’ jurisdiction over the behind-the-meter load itself, the Commission abso-
lutely can take action to ensure its North Star principles that such facilities do not (1) impact the 
safety or reliability of the bulk electric system, and (2) do not create conditions for improper sub-
sidization by network customers. PJM and PPL Electric sought to use the limited tools available 
 
18 See PJM Answer at 27–28.  
19 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Comments of the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission, Docket 
Nos. EL25-49-000 et al. (Apr. 22, 2025) at 3 (“it is well-established in Pennsylvania law that when elec-
tric service is provided to a ‘defined, privileged and limited group’ it is not provided ‘to or for the pub-
lic,’” quoting Drexelbrook Assocs. v. Pennsylvania Pub. Util. Comm’n, 212 A.2d 237, 240 (Pa. 1965)).  
PPL Electric is of course aware of the age of some of the Pennsylvania judicial rulings that set forth this 
legal position and the significant developments in electric service and electricity markets that have 
changed the underlying fact patterns since then. To PPL Electric’s knowledge, no Pennsylvania court has 
been presented with the question of retail jurisdiction over a large generator located behind the meter of a 
wholesale generator. All parties should proceed with the understanding that state law can change based on 
these new conditions.  
20 The fact pattern laid out in the Show Cause Order on this point is not entirely correct. PPL Electric did 
not “allow[] a generator in its service territory to enter into a co-location arrangement.” Show Cause Or-
der at ¶ 75. PPL Electric had no ability to withhold permission.  
21 PJM Answer at 29–31.

8 
 
to them, specifically the non-standard terms and conditions schedule of the Susquehanna ISA, to 
improve an initially bad setup. Following the Commission’s denial of that effort, PPL Electric 
remains in agreement with PJM that the Commission should clarify its rules to ensure the tariffs 
it regulates do not allow behind-the-meter load to create the negative impact on the transmission 
system that existed at Susquehanna.  
PPL Electric responds to the Options laid out in the PJM Answer below:  
1. 
Options 1 – 3  
 
As PJM recognizes, Options 1 – 3 already exist in the Tariff and are available options for 
load seeking to interconnect. PPL Electric agrees that Option 1 (which can be considered the de-
fault for all load in its territory) and Option 2 (where load is at the same point of interconnection 
as a generator but metered separately) are the preferred options. They do not impact safety or re-
liability and do not create any subsidization concerns—although PJM’s caveats regarding the 
scale of data center load sharing a point of interconnection are important.22 Neither Option re-
quires any tariff changes to accommodate.  
 
As laid out by PJM in Option 3, the PJM Tariff already accommodates generation behind 
the meter of network load. This arrangement is more complicated than “normal” load purchasing 
exclusively from the PJM markets, but behind-the-meter generation has generally proven to 
work within the existing system and PPL Electric is not opposed to it. As PJM recognizes, be-
hind the meter generation at an existing load differs both in kind and degree from load appearing 
behind the meter of an existing generator, especially when attempted at the scale of a data center.  
 
22 See PJM Answer at 13, Note 5.

9 
 
2. 
Options 4, 5 
 
PJM’s Options 4 and 5 reflect a good faith attempt to accommodate a behind-the-meter 
load at an existing wholesale generator. PJM considers them “less preferred,” but recognizes that 
where retail load interconnects and is metered is a question of state law, beyond the ability of the 
local utility, regional transmission organization, or FERC to control.23 Specifically, these options 
reflect lessons learned through the Susquehanna ISA negotiations. Incorporating Options 4 and 
potentially 5 into the PJM Tariff would largely formalize the ad-hoc structure at Susquehanna 
without the need to reopen the most controversial portions of the Susquehanna ISA (although 
certain protections and physical interconnection changes may still need to be incorporated into 
that agreement). Making these tariff changes with no negative impact on reliability or cost subsi-
dization will be difficult though, as behind-the-meter load is fundamentally less visible and less 
interactive with the grid than “normal” front-of-meter load.24 PPL Electric thus agrees that these 
options are not the preferred way forward, but may still be necessary where state law requires ac-
commodation of behind-the-meter load.25  
 
Option 4 would accommodate co-located load behind the meter of a wholesale generator. 
It requires “protection mechanisms … to prevent delivery of energy from the grid to serve the 
load in the event the generation is offline.”26 Ensuring such protection mechanisms were in place 
was PPL Electric’s goal in amending the Susquehanna ISA in 2024.27 Specifically, the 
 
23 See PJM Answer at 14.  
24 See PPL Electric TC Comments at 9–12 (large loads should interconnect in front of the meter to max-
imize reliability and minimize cost shifts).  
25 See id. at 12–15 (the Commission cannot regulate the retail relationship, but should set wholesale tariff 
rules that remove the incentive to locate behind the meter).  
26 PJM Answer at 14. 
27 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Motion for Leave to Answer Protest and Answer of PPL Electric 
Utilities Corporation, Docket No. ER24-2172 (Jul. 12, 2024) (“PPL ISA Answer”) at 3 (“PPL’s main goal 
in amending the ISA was to ensure the reliability of the PJM transmission system and to protect PPL’s

10 
 
unamended agreement did not adequately provide for real-time metering and telemetry of the be-
hind-the-meter load, did not prevent additional backup generators being interconnected, did not 
adequately ensure separation of load in the case of loss of generation, did not condition recon-
nection of the load on PJM or PPL Electric’s approval following an outage, and did not require 
PPL Electric be given an opportunity to review changes to the operating procedure of the behind-
the-meter load, among others.28 These ISA changes were necessary because the configuration at 
Susquehanna (and envisioned by PJM as Option 4) “carries operational risk.”29 Specifically, this 
configuration risks “large, unplanned, unmodeled” load appearing instantaneously on the system 
if the protection mechanisms fail.30 At the scale of a data center, this risk is significant and the 
Commission’s concern with such a setup is well-placed.31  
 
Because the Commission denied the amendments to the Susquehanna ISA on other 
grounds,32 the PJM Tariff still does not include sufficient protections against load appearing 
 
customers.”). See also, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of PPL 
Electric Utilities Corporation, Docket No. ER24-2172 (Oct. 9, 2024) at 2–3 (“PPL’s position in favor of 
the ISA amendments at issue here should not be interpreted as anything other than its belief that those 
amendments improve the reliability of the transmission grid and protect PPL’s and other customers from 
potential negative effects caused by the customer’s behind-the-meter facility.”).  
28 See PPL ISA Answer at 4–6.  
29 PJM Answer at 14.  
30 PPL Electric TC Comments at 10–11.  
31 See Order to Show Cause at ¶ 83 (“We are also concerned about the reliability and resource adequacy 
implications of co-location arrangements. … we are concerned that the Tariff may be unjust and unrea-
sonable and unduly discriminatory or preferential insofar as it lacks rules necessary to provide PJM with 
sufficient information to perform appropriate analysis to ensure reliable system operations given the char-
acteristics of co-location arrangements.”). 
32 ISA Rejection Order at ¶ 87 (finding the proposed provisions that “mirror provisions that PJM has in-
cluded in the PJM Guidance Document, do not meet the requisite standard” for non-conforming provi-
sions), id. at ¶ 88 (leaving “multiple important questions unresolved,” including the specific non-con-
forming provisions proposed in the Susquehanna ISA); but see Phillips (dissenting) at ¶ 1 (“we are reject-
ing protections that the interconnected transmission owner says will enhance reliability while also creat-
ing unnecessary roadblocks to an industry that is necessary for our national security”).

11 
 
instantaneously on the system due to an inadvertent loss of generation in a behind-the-meter load 
arrangement as laid out in Option 4 or as continues to exist at Susquehanna. PPL Electric thus 
agrees strongly with PJM that “Tariff modifications would be needed” to move forward with Op-
tion 4.33 Should the Commission agree, it should focus on its clear jurisdiction over the genera-
tor—not the retail behind-the-meter load itself which is regulated by the state. The PJM Tariff 
can be amended to incorporate the North Star principles, compelling the generator to prevent any 
impact on the safety or reliability of the transmission grid and to prevent subsidization of the 
load by network customers. In all likelihood, these protections will reduce the incentive for large 
loads to locate behind-the-meter in the first place, but the option will formally remain for them in 
states that allow it.  
 
PPL Electric’s concerns with behind-the-meter load are perhaps even more acute under 
Option 5, where the load can also “receive back-up service from the grid.”34 PJM insists that any 
such approval to “take back-up power from the grid would be subject to conditions” related to 
reliability, and would require “real-time, bespoke operational decision-making to determine 
whether load can continue to be served.”35 Imposing these conditions and establishing the au-
thority for this decision-making would clearly require Tariff changes. Under Pennsylvania law 
PPL Electric cannot deny backup service properly requested under its General Tariff, which 
 
33 Such modifications could include changes to the pro forma ISA.  
34 PJM Answer at 14–15.  
35 Id.

12 
 
allows for both backup36 and temporary37 service. These rules also apply to behind-the-meter 
customers who can properly take service under the General Tariff (although doing so requires a 
meter, changing the nature of the load). To be sure, for PJM to condition such service as pro-
posed, “Tariff modifications would be needed.”38  
 
PPL Electric reiterates that Options 4 and 5 are not preferred. Even if properly governed 
under the PJM Tariff, they offer less reliability than other methods of interconnecting co-located 
load. They also risk subsidization of the behind-the-meter load by network customers, as was 
highlighted by protests in the Susquehanna ISA docket39 and commentators to the technical con-
ference, including PPL Electric.40 Nevertheless, Pennsylvania and some other PJM states allow 
at least some form of behind-the-meter load and the PJM Tariff may need clarification or amend-
ment to accommodate them. PPL Electric thus joins PJM in calling for increased clarity from the 
Commission here.

customers who have another source of power which can be substituted for Company’s service for any of 
customer's operations”).  
37 PPL Electric Utilities Corporation General Tariff, Rule 7, available at https://www.pplelectric.com/-

used solely for a service that is known to be limited in duration.”).   
38 PJM Answer at 15.  
39 See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Declaration of John J. Reed and Danielle S. Powers in Support 
of Protest of Exelon Corporation and American Electric Power Services Corporation, Docket No. ER24-

could encourage other generators and large consumers to pursue similar arrangements, leading to wide-
spread cross-subsidization issues and leaving unresolved questions of cost responsibility for grid use.”).  
40 See, e.g., PPL Electric TC Comments at 14 (“An equitable energy market requires that this load not re-
ceive power and grid services subsidized by other customers on the grid. It also requires that the generator 
not be able to capture a portion of this subsidy by selling at a premium to its private customer.).

13 
 
3. 
Options 6–8  
PJM’s other Options are less controversial, but are also less directly relevant to the ques-
tions raised regarding how the PJM Tariff should address co-located load behind-the-meter of a 
large wholesale generator. All three remaining Options instead primarily focus on the larger is-
sue of resource adequacy. As PPL Electric explained in its Post-Technical Conference Com-
ments, data center growth is critical for economic development and will require new generation 
and market adjustments.41  
Option 6 would incentivize data centers to “Bring Your Own Generation” by speeding 
the interconnection process for those new generators if they serve as capacity resources. This 
proposal mirrors the Reliability Resource Initiative (“RRI”) currently in progress.42 PJM is fac-
ing significant resource adequacy concerns and speeding the interconnection process for genera-
tion resources that can help is likely to be a beneficial step. Although this option appears to be 
independent from questions around co-located load, PPL Electric generally supports it.  
 
Option 7 would allow large loads to integrate as non-capacity backed load and avoid ca-
pacity costs so long as the load is willing to curtail earlier in the stack to support reliability dur-
ing emergency conditions. PPL Electric reserves comment on this option as there are not suffi-
cient details in the PJM filing to understand the potential changes necessary to the PJM Tariff or 
any potential conflicts with state law. Finally, Option 8 recognizes that co-located loads have the 
ability to provide demand response under the existing PJM Tariff and offers potential changes to 
 
41 See id. at 1–2 (“Robust data center development is critical to keeping the United States at the forefront 
of information technology development and to protect national security.”), 15 (“new data centers will tie 
up generation and impact resource adequacy regardless of whether they are located behind-the-meter”).  
42 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Tariff Revisions for Reliability Resource Initiative, Docket No. 
ER25-712 (Dec. 13, 2024); accepted Order Accepting Tariff Revisions, 190 FERC ¶ 61,084 (Feb. 11, 
2025) (speeding interconnection process for certain capacity additions by adding them to existing queue).

14 
 
the rules that could make this more attractive. Again, PPL Electric reserves comment as there are 
not sufficient details to understand the proposed changes from the existing rules under the PJM 
Tariff or their potential impacts on the transmission system and energy markets.  
B. 
Responses to PSEG  
 
PSE&G argues that the Commission should apply cost allocation rules developed in dis-
putes between different transmission zones to the newly presented question of how transmission 
costs should be allocated among retail customers in a single transmission zone.43 It argues such a 
rule would require transmission charges “be assessed based on a party’s ‘actual use’ of the trans-
mission system.44 This would trample on state jurisdiction over retail rates, which governs allo-
cation of transmission costs to retail customers. It would require FERC to recognize a new class 
of retail customer and then direct the states how to assign transmission costs (assessed to the 
transmission zone via Schedule 12 of the PJM Tariff) among these retail rate classes. PSE&G’s 
proposal would also violate a longstanding tenet of FERC law, which “consistently reject[s] cost 
causation arguments made by network customers that [seek] to lower their load ratio share based 
on actual use of the transmission system.”45 The Commission should reject this argument.  
C. 
Response to AES Ohio 
PPL Electric agrees with AES Ohio that, while the PJM Tariff “remains just and reasona-
ble as to service … co-located load take[s],” there are potentially other solutions, especially in 
states willing to accommodate behind-the-meter load.46 As explained above, state law 
 
43 PSE&G Answer at 11 and Note 24.  
44 Id. at 11.  
45 National Railroad Passenger Corporation v. PPL Electric Utilities Corporation and PJM Interconnec-
tion, L.L.C., Order Denying Complaint, 171 FERC ¶ 61,237, Docket No. EL19-78 (Jun. 18, 2020) at ¶ 41.  
46 AES Ohio Answer at 1–2.

15 
 
determines whether or not to allow behind-the-meter retail load. The PJM Tariff must accommo-
date whatever choice the states make, but in doing so it must ensure (a) the safety and reliability 
of the transmission system is protected, and (b) that costs are not transferred from the behind the 
meter load to the network load.  
IV. 
CONCLUSION 
 
For the reasons stated above and in the Comments of the Indicated PJM Transmission 
Owners, PPL Electric respectfully requests the Commission accept this Answer, find the existing 
PJM Tariff just and reasonable, and provide additional clarification regarding the treatment of 
behind-the-meter co-located load as it determines necessary.
